source.title: Repeat After Me: Transformers are Better than State Space Models at Copying
source.authors: Samy Jelassi; David Brandfonbrener; S. Kakade; Eran Malach

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests n-gram lookup and copying behaviours related to induction, but does not identify or causally test induction heads or their formation.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly calls suffix-key n-gram lookup closely related to induction heads and tests n-gram retrieval behaviour. It does not inspect attention heads, previous-token-head composition, training-time formation, loss bumps, or loss-by-token in-context learning. Other copying, retrieval, and QA results are not catalogued here because they do not test a listed version’s specific induction-head claim.
record.test_reason: The paper never identifies attention heads, previous-token-head composition, training dynamics or loss-by-token in-context learning. It measures task accuracy on copying and n-gram lookup, which it calls 'closely related to induction heads'. That is a related behaviour-level construct, not a test of any version. Hard-ALiBi also hard-codes previous-token-style local heads by design, so any composition is imposed rather than shown to arise.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Authors conclude transformers are better than GSSMs at copying and retrieving from context, in theory (two-layer construction vs a state-size lower bound) and in practice, including pretrained Pythia vs Mamba. They also conclude trained transformers use n-gram hashing-style lookup. They mention induction heads only as related prior work and do not identify them.
record.recipe_differences: Tests copying and suffix-/prefix-key n-gram lookup behaviour, rather than measuring induction heads or their composition with previous-token heads.
record.method_sensitivity: Task variant and positional encoding affect lookup performance: GSSMs do well on prefix-key lookup; Hard-Alibi generalizes better than NoPE and Alibi in the reported comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: Transformers trained from scratch generalize on suffix-key n-gram lookup and copying far better than Mamba and LSTM. A Hard-ALiBi transformer's copying degrades with duplicated n-grams of length ≥5 and matches a perfect 5-gram model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformers, but not fixed-state models (SSMs, RNNs), learn induction-like n-gram match-and-copy retrieval that length-generalizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretrained Pythia outperforms Mamba of similar size on copying natural-language and random strings, phone-book lookup, and SQuAD as context grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretrained transformers outperform pretrained SSMs on in-context copying and retrieval.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235 (2024)
record.problems: No induction-head identification or causal head intervention; the tested transformer is not stated to be attention-only. The relevant n-gram lookup results are shown in figures, and no numerical values or uncertainty estimates for those results are stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Copying, phone-book lookup, natural-language copying, and SQuAD question-answering results were left out because they do not test a listed version’s specific induction-head or loss-by-token claim. See Figures 1, 5–7 and 10.

untested.parts: Head identification, attention patterns, previous-token-head composition, attention-only models
All: no training-time formation, abruptness or loss bump
All: no loss-by-token-index or attribution to heads
Presence of induction heads across models or architectures; only task accuracy is compared
All: no comparison of head types for few-shot learning

missing.what: Pretrained Pythia vs Mamba results on copying, phone-book lookup and SQuAD. Relevant only to the related copying construct, not to a version.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1 labels are reclassified. Behavioural lookup accuracy in a 12-layer transformer with MLPs, with hard-coded local heads in Hard-ALiBi, cannot bear on head formation or composition. Prefix-key rows are not even induction-style tasks.

versions.untested_parts: Tests induction-like n-gram lookup behaviour, not whether induction heads form, their attention pattern, composition with previous-token heads, or the claim specifically in attention-only transformers.
No measurement of induction-head formation over training, abruptness, training loss bump, or aligned in-context-learning gain.
No measurement of most in-context learning as loss falling with token index, or attribution of that behaviour to induction heads in large transformers.
Compares architectures on copying and lookup, but does not measure whether induction-behaviour heads appear across families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
Does not test how data or training setup changes induction-head formation or in-context-learning persistence.
Few-shot retrieval and QA are evaluated, but the study does not compare induction heads with other heads or mechanisms as carriers of few-shot task learning.
No measurement of sub-steps or multiple transitions in induction-head formation.

rows.subject: Transformer (Hard-Alibi)
rows.operation_detail: Tested on suffix-key n-gram lookup after training on strings of length at most 30.
rows.note: The text says transformers perform well, with a relatively small performance drop as length increases to 100. The plot separates positional-encoding variants.
rows.check: Suffix-key lookup accuracy for a 12-layer GPT-NeoX with MLPs (not attention-only). No head identified. Measures task behaviour, not the V1 mechanism. Figure-only value.

rows.operation_detail: Tested on suffix-key n-gram lookup after training on strings of length at most 30.
rows.note: The text describes transformer performance as good overall with a relatively small drop; it does not give a separate textual result for NoPE.
rows.check: Same as R1, NoPE variant. No separate textual value.

rows.subject: Transformer (Hard-Alibi)
rows.operation_detail: Tested on prefix-key n-gram lookup after training on strings of length at most 30.
rows.note: The text says GSSMs achieve perfect length generalization on this variant, and outperform NoPE and Alibi transformers but not Hard-Alibi.
rows.check: Prefix-key lookup does not require induction-style retrieval; the paper says the key can be matched on the fly. Not bearing on any version.

rows.subject: Transformer (Hard-Alibi)
rows.operation_detail: Tested copying on sequences deliberately containing a duplicated n-gram.
rows.note: The text says accuracy remains roughly the same for n ≤ 4.
rows.check: Duplicated-n-gram copying probes the copy algorithm's n-gram length, not induction-head formation or composition. Hard-ALiBi forces local attention heads by design.

rows.subject: Transformer (Hard-Alibi)
rows.operation_detail: Tested copying on sequences deliberately containing a duplicated n-gram.
rows.note: The text says accuracy starts dropping when inputs contain duplicated sequences of 5 or more tokens; the authors say this suggests reliance on roughly 5-gram retrieval.
rows.check: Same as R11. The drop at n≥5 indicates roughly 5-gram retrieval behaviour, not a head mechanism.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Hard-Alibi transformer on duplicated-n-gram copying and tested n-gram lookup
reader_labels.reason: The transformer shows the reported n-gram retrieval behaviour: accuracy is maintained for duplicated n-grams of length 2–4 and suffix-key lookup generalizes with a relatively small drop (R1, R11). The paper does not establish the head mechanism itself.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Performance depends on task variant and positional encoding: GSSMs achieve perfect prefix-key length generalization, outperforming NoPE and Alibi transformers, though not Hard-Alibi (R6–R10). This limits the behavioural comparison, not the untested head-composition claim.
